about: Threat models as plain text (doc 133, principle `threat-model`). Think like the attacker before you build: for every component that crosses a trust boundary, list its parts, its data flows and where trust changes, then say what could go wrong for each part in all six STRIDE ways. Each threat is mitigated with proof (an evidence file that exists), accepted with a reason and a review date that has not passed, or ruled out with a reason. Draw the diagram in any tool you like (the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon, a whiteboard); this file is what the repository keeps, because a binary model file cannot be checked and a public repository should not hold one. Fitness `threat-modelled` holds the structure, the evidence and the dates; the number of models only goes up.

command-door.name: The hosted Command Center door and each node's /_door.json
command-door.scope: A static page that lists a person's machines and asks each whether it is up; the one path each node answers itself.
boundaries: the internet between the page and a machine
a link sent by someone else

flows.data: GET /_door.json: no cookie, no body
flows.crosses: the internet

flows.data: a list of addresses in a link
flows.crosses: a link sent by someone else

flows.data: the page's own code
flows.crosses: the static site host

threats.threat: A crafted link adds a machine the attacker controls, so the person opens a look-alike Command Center.
threats.mitigation: the link only shows what it wants to add and waits for a yes; only https addresses or this device are accepted; nothing but a plain GET is ever sent to a listed machine

threats.threat: Something that is not the machine (a dead tunnel's error page, a look-alike) answers the status check, so a dead machine reads as up.
threats.mitigation: a machine counts as up only on one exact sentence, readable cross-origin; both false-green cases are tested

threats.threat: A malformed, oversized or prototype-polluting link corrupts the list.
threats.mitigation: every field is rebuilt from validated parts; the list is capped; garbage is ignored

threats.threat: The host, or the account that publishes to it, is compromised and serves altered page code.
threats.reason: The page holds no keys and sends only credential-free requests, so the damage is a wrong machine address; the account is protected and the apps move to a host that applies headers.

threats.threat: A person denies an action the door took for them.
threats.reason: The door performs no action on anyone's behalf: it only lists and links; the machine it opens keeps its own audit.

threats.threat: The list of machines or the visit leaks to a third party.
threats.mitigation: no request leaves except to a listed machine, without cookies or referrer; a strict content policy forbids anything else

threats.threat: Another site on the same browser origin reads the list from storage.
threats.reason: The list holds addresses only (no keys or passwords), and the shared origin is removed by hosting the apps on an origin of their own.

threats.threat: A hostile or hung machine stalls the page or floods it.
threats.mitigation: a four-second timeout, a cap on the number of machines, and a fifteen-second interval only while the page is visible

threats.threat: Text from a link or a machine becomes script in the page.
threats.mitigation: text is only ever set as text, never as markup; no inline script is allowed by the policy; a test forbids innerHTML and its relatives

kit-lock.name: The app lock in every kit app (Vantage first): device biometrics, encryption at rest, a recovery phrase
kit-lock.scope: A person's data in the browser on their own device, locked behind the device's Face ID, fingerprint or Windows Hello (WebAuthn, user verification), encrypted at rest where the browser supports the PRF extension.
boundaries: the person's device and its authenticator
the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: a user-verified assertion and the PRF secret for this app's salt
flows.crosses: the person's device and its authenticator

flows.data: every value except four device keys, AES-GCM encrypted under a random data key
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: credential id, salts, the data key wrapped twice (biometric, phrase)
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: the phrase typed by the person, PBKDF2 310,000 rounds
flows.crosses: the person's device and its authenticator

flows.data: the person's values, only while unlocked
flows.crosses: the estate's sync service

threats.threat: Someone else at the device (a family member, staff, a thief with the unlocked phone) opens the app and reads everything.
threats.mitigation: the app opens only after a user-verified biometric or the device PIN; a different face or device gets a different PRF secret, which unwraps nothing

threats.threat: Reading the browser's storage directly (devtools, a copied profile, disk forensics) exposes the person's data in plain text.
threats.mitigation: with PRF every value is AES-GCM encrypted under a random data key that only the biometric or the recovery phrase can unwrap; only language, theme, discreet setting and the lock record stay plain

threats.threat: A glance at the screen or the phone's app switcher shows private content after the person looked away.
threats.mitigation: the screen is veiled while hidden and the app locks after being away longer than the chosen time (1, 5 or 15 minutes)

threats.threat: On a browser without PRF the lock is only a screen gate, so the stored data is readable by anyone with the device's browser profile and the know-how.
threats.reason: PRF is in current Chrome, Edge, Android and Safari 18 and later; on an older browser a screen gate still stops the casual look, and the app says plainly that the data itself is not encrypted, so the person can choose another browser

threats.threat: A sync while locked writes the estate's plain copy over the encrypted values, or pushes a copy of nulls that wipes the synced data.
threats.mitigation: no push, pull or merge runs while locked; sync resumes after unlock

threats.threat: Someone edits the lock record to switch the lock off or point it at their own credential.
threats.mitigation: the data key is wrapped, not stored: a changed record unwraps nothing, the data stays encrypted, and turning the lock off is possible only while unlocked

threats.threat: The person cannot tell whether their data on this device is really encrypted or only behind a screen.
threats.mitigation: Settings states the mode in plain words: encrypted, or screen lock only

threats.threat: A new phone, a reset fingerprint or a broken sensor locks the person out of their own data for good.
threats.mitigation: a one-time recovery phrase (20 base32 characters, PBKDF2 310,000 rounds) wraps the same data key; the encrypted backup and sync remain as before

threats.threat: A write made just before the tab closes is lost, because encryption is asynchronous.
threats.reason: each write is encrypted within milliseconds and queued in order; losing the last keystroke when a tab is killed mid-write is the same risk the app had before, and the undo and sync copies remain

threats.threat: Script injected into the page while unlocked reads the decrypted values from memory.
threats.mitigation: the kit renders every value through one escape helper and uses data-a actions instead of inline code, and the hosted apps carry a strict content security policy; encryption protects data at rest, not a compromised running page

hosted-apps.name: The hosted Life OS and Vantage, with OneDrive sync
hosted-apps.scope: Single-file apps served from a static host, holding a person's data on the device and an encrypted copy in their own OneDrive.

flows.data: an encrypted copy of the person's data
flows.crosses: Microsoft's sign-in and OneDrive

flows.data: the app's own code
flows.crosses: the static site host

threats.threat: A look-alike copy of the app asks for the Microsoft sign-in.
threats.mitigation: the sign-in only returns to addresses allow-listed in the person's own app registration

threats.threat: The OneDrive copy is altered or rolled back.
threats.mitigation: authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM); a copy that would wipe most of the data is refused

threats.threat: Two devices edit and nobody can say which change came from where.
threats.reason: Sync merges per key by last writer and keeps no per-edit audit; for one person's own data this is a convenience loss, not a control gap.

threats.threat: Microsoft, or anyone who gets the file, reads the person's data.
threats.mitigation: the copy is encrypted on the device with a key from the person's passphrase, which never leaves the device

threats.threat: Other sites on the same browser origin, and a host that sends no security headers, expose the stored data to framing and storage reads.
threats.reason: GitHub Pages ignores the header file and shares one origin per account; header rules are written and an origin of its own is dated.

threats.threat: The static host is down, so the app cannot load.
threats.mitigation: every device keeps its own copy through a service worker; the app opens with the host down and with no network

threats.threat: Script injected into the single-file app reads the data and the sign-in tokens.
threats.reason: The app carries inline code, so a strict script policy is not yet possible; framing and plugins are forbidden and the app's own origin plus a nonce policy are dated.

lifeos-backup.name: The Life OS backup file: encrypted by default with a device-kept backup phrase
lifeos-backup.scope: The whole Life OS saved to one file that leaves the browser (Downloads, a cloud folder, a chat), and restored on this or another device.
boundaries: the browser's storage for this app
the device's file system and anything that copies files off it

flows.data: every value except sync keys and the phrase, AES-256-GCM under a key from the phrase (PBKDF2-SHA256, 310,000 rounds, random salt and IV)
flows.crosses: the device's file system and anything that copies files off it

flows.data: a 100-bit phrase made on the device, kept under a device-only key that no sync or backup carries
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: the phrase typed on a new device to restore
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

threats.threat: The backup in Downloads is read by another app, a photo or file cloud sync, or whoever receives it in a chat, and exposes the family's whole life.
threats.mitigation: the file is ciphertext only; without the phrase it opens nothing

threats.threat: The phrase travels with the data (inside the file, the estate sync or the OneDrive copy), so whoever gets one gets both.
threats.mitigation: the phrase lives under a gm_sync_od key that every sync path and every backup skips, and is removed from any restored set

threats.threat: Someone edits the backup so that a restore plants false data (a changed nominee, a wrong account).
threats.mitigation: AES-GCM authenticates the whole file; any change fails to open

threats.threat: A file made to look like a backup is restored, or a guessed phrase opens a real one.
threats.mitigation: a wrong phrase opens nothing; 100 random bits behind 310,000 PBKDF2 rounds cannot be guessed; the restore asks before it overwrites

threats.threat: A readable copy is made and later nobody can tell when or from which device.
threats.mitigation: every backup and every readable copy is written to Who touched my data with time and device; a readable copy is flagged in red with what to delete

threats.threat: The phone is lost and the person never saved the phrase, so the encrypted backup cannot be opened.
threats.reason: the phrase is shown at the first backup with Copy and is in Settings under Backup phrase at any time; the OneDrive or estate sync copy restores without it; a readable copy stays available by name for a person who chooses it

threats.threat: A malicious backup file (or a synced device) plants markup in the profile, and a screen that shows the profile runs it (stored XSS). The 2026-11-11 audit found four profile fields that did.
threats.mitigation: the profile is cleaned of < > " ` at the one door every read and write passes (load/store); a fuzz of every tab and 85 typed fields ran no planted script; every restore keeps an undo snapshot

threat-news.name: Threats in the news: open-source headlines ranking the Life OS's red-team drills
threat-news.scope: intel/threatwatch.py reads public news and security feeds on the build server, matches titles to the curated threat library, and publishes intel.json next to the hosted Life OS, which shows the top threat and its drills.
boundaries: the public internet (news sites, feeds, search)
the hosted site that serves intel.json
the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: RSS titles, dates and links only
flows.crosses: the public internet (news sites, feeds, search)

flows.data: each curated pattern with its drills, ranked by heat x severity, plus up to three headlines
flows.crosses: the hosted site that serves intel.json

flows.data: heat, order and headlines for ids the app already knows
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: which drills were rehearsed, and when (kept on the device)
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

threats.threat: A fake news site or a spoofed feed plants stories to steer what a person rehearses, or to scare them into an action.
threats.mitigation: news only ranks a pattern and links evidence; every drill comes from the curated library in the repository, reviewed like code; a link off the source's own hosts is dropped

threats.threat: intel.json is changed on the host or in transit to rewrite a drill (for example 'send money to verify'), add a fake threat or rank one falsely.
threats.mitigation: the app takes only heat, order and headlines from the pack; drills, names and stories come from the copy bundled in the app; unknown ids are ignored; numbers and text are capped

threats.threat: A headline is later edited or removed, and nobody can tell what the app showed.
threats.reason: the pack is a public file rebuilt daily from public sources; each headline keeps its outlet and date and links to the original; no decision rests on a headline, only on the curated drill

threats.threat: Fetching threat news from the phone reveals what a person worries about (kidnap, a honeytrap) to news sites and trackers.
threats.mitigation: all fetching happens on the build server; the phone reads one static file from its own origin, the same file for everyone, and sends no profile; rehearsals stay on the device

threats.threat: A huge feed, an entity-expansion bomb or a dead source stops the daily build, or the state grows without limit.
threats.mitigation: the shared RSS reader caps size at 4 MB and refuses DTDs and entities; each source fails alone; a failed fetch never fails the site build; the state keeps at most 2,000 items for 120 days

threats.threat: A headline carries markup or a javascript: link that runs in the Life OS (XSS) with the person's data.
threats.mitigation: every text is escaped; only https links are kept, opened with noopener and noreferrer; markup from a headline is shown as text

lifeos-lock.name: The Life OS privacy lock: device biometrics before the app shows anything
lifeos-lock.scope: A person turns on the lock in Ops; the Life OS then opens behind a full-screen lock that only the device's own fingerprint, face or Windows Hello (a WebAuthn platform credential, user verification required) or a one-time recovery code removes; it locks after time away and veils itself when hidden.
boundaries: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: a WebAuthn get with a fresh random challenge and user verification required
flows.crosses: the device's platform authenticator

flows.data: the credential id, the idle time and the recovery code's PBKDF2 hash (310,000 rounds, random salt); never the code
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

threats.threat: Someone holding the unlocked phone, a family member or a colleague opens the Life OS and reads everything.
threats.mitigation: with the lock on, the app opens behind a full-screen lock and everything behind it is hidden until the device's own biometric or the recovery code is given

threats.threat: The app switcher or a glance over the shoulder shows the person's money, family and plans.
threats.mitigation: when the app is hidden the screen is veiled; after the chosen idle time it locks

threats.threat: A changed fingerprint or a reset of the device's biometrics locks the person out of their own life.
threats.mitigation: a one-time 16-character recovery code, shown once at set-up, opens the app; only its hash is stored

threats.threat: Someone with developer tools on the unlocked device deletes the lock record or edits the page to skip the lock.
threats.reason: the lock guards the screen against a person holding the device, not against someone already controlling the browser; the data on the device is protected by the phone's own lock and storage encryption, and backups are encrypted; encryption at rest inside the Life OS is the next slice (queue app-lock)

threats.threat: A lock is removed and nobody can tell when.
threats.reason: turning the lock off needs the app to be unlocked and a confirmation; a single-person, on-device app keeps no audit trail of its own settings; revisit with the enterprise edition

threats.threat: A stored recovery code or credential lets an attacker unlock from a copy of the device data.
threats.mitigation: the code is never stored, only a salted PBKDF2 hash; the credential id alone cannot sign a WebAuthn challenge without the device's authenticator

lifeos-share-in.name: Share into the Life OS: a message from another app becomes numbers, on the device
lifeos-share-in.scope: From any app (Messages, mail, a bank app) the person shares an SMS or text to the installed Life OS, or pastes it; the Life OS reads EPF, NPS, fund, bank-balance and card-bill amounts and offers to save them with one tap. Also the card guide: which card to use when, from each card's name and statement day.
boundaries: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: shared title and text, at most 20,000 characters
flows.crosses: the phone's share sheet (other apps)

flows.data: the text, held in a local cache entry and deleted once read; never sent over the network
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: amounts the person chose to save, with their date; card names and statement days only
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

threats.threat: Another app shares a forged message (a fake balance) to skew the person's numbers.
threats.mitigation: nothing is saved by sharing: the app shows what it found and where it would go, and only the person's tap saves it

threats.threat: Shared text crafted as markup or script runs inside the Life OS.
threats.mitigation: shared text is only ever shown escaped, never inserted as HTML, and only numbers are extracted

threats.threat: A saved number cannot be traced to when it was saved.
threats.mitigation: every saved amount carries its date and shows 'updated N days ago'

threats.threat: A bank SMS travels to the web host inside the share link and is logged there.
threats.mitigation: the service worker answers the share link on the device and never forwards it; the text goes to a local cache entry, which the app deletes after reading

threats.threat: A card number, CVV or expiry date is typed into the card guide and kept on the device.
threats.mitigation: the card guide stores only a card's name and statement day and refuses any input with a run of 12 or more digits

threats.threat: A huge shared text freezes the app.
threats.mitigation: shared text is cut to 20,000 characters before it is read

threats.threat: Shared text triggers an action in the app (a delete, a sync) without the person.
threats.reason: the reader has no actions but 'save this amount', and only a tap by the person saves

estate-sms-inbox.name: The estate's SMS inbox: bank messages forwarded from the phone, read by the Life OS
estate-sms-inbox.scope: An open-source SMS forwarder on the person's phone posts messages from bank senders to estate-sync (POST /sync/inbox/sms) over Tailscale; they are stored in the person's own state as gm_sms_inbox and read by the Life OS on its next sync, which then clears them.

flows.data: sender id and message text, at most 8 KB, with a write-only token
flows.crosses: the private network (Tailscale)

flows.data: bank-sender messages only, one-time codes dropped, digit runs of 12 or more masked, at most 300 for 14 days
flows.crosses: the estate's sync store

flows.data: the inbox key, through the device-token sync
flows.crosses: the private network (Tailscale)

threats.threat: Someone on the network posts forged bank messages to skew the person's numbers.
threats.mitigation: a separate inbox token is required (compared in constant time), the door is pinned to one user, and it is reachable only on the person's private network

threats.threat: Two messages arriving together overwrite each other, or overwrite the person's other data.
threats.mitigation: each append runs under the same write lock as every state write and touches only the inbox key

threats.threat: A number cannot be traced to the message it came from.
threats.mitigation: every message carries its sender and time; the Life OS saves each amount with its date

threats.threat: One-time codes, card numbers or personal SMS are kept on the estate.
threats.mitigation: only senders shaped like bank sender ids are kept, one-time codes are never stored, digit runs of 12 or more are masked, and the Life OS clears the inbox after reading, so the texts leave the store on the next sync

threats.threat: A leaked forwarder token exposes the person's Life OS data.
threats.mitigation: the inbox token is write-only: it is not a device token and cannot read state

threats.threat: A flood of messages fills the store or slows the estate.
threats.mitigation: 8 KB per message, 60 a minute per token, at most 300 messages for 14 days

threats.threat: The inbox is used to write any other key of the person's state.
threats.mitigation: the endpoint writes only the inbox key; its body is never merged as state

estate-web-push.name: Web push from the estate: the Life OS's own alerts, with nothing to install
estate-web-push.scope: estate-sync makes its own VAPID key (0600, beside its database); a paired Life OS fetches the public key and, after one Allow tap, posts the browser's push subscription; ./securax notify sends through 'python -m syncsvc.push send' inside the container, encrypted per device (RFC 8291) and signed (RFC 8292), to the browser's push service, which wakes the phone.

flows.data: the browser's subscription (endpoint, its public key, auth secret), with the device token
flows.crosses: the private network (Tailscale)

flows.data: at most 10 subscriptions a person, push-service hosts only
flows.crosses: the estate's sync store

flows.data: a title and one short line (counts and labels), encrypted for the device, with a 12-hour VAPID signature
flows.crosses: the browser vendor's push service

threats.threat: Someone without a paired device subscribes and receives the person's alerts.
threats.mitigation: the key and subscribe endpoints take the device token or the signed-in identity, pinned to the person's own user

threats.threat: Someone else sends pushes that look like the estate's.
threats.mitigation: the subscription is bound to the estate's VAPID key; the push service accepts only messages signed with it, and the private key never leaves the estate

threats.threat: A subscription is planted that points the estate at an internal address (request forgery).
threats.mitigation: only plain https endpoints on the browsers' push services are kept (no other host, port or credentials), and redirects are never followed

threats.threat: An alert cannot be traced to what sent it.
threats.mitigation: every alert comes from ./securax notify, which keeps undelivered ones in its dead-letter file and prints each channel's result

threats.threat: The browser vendor's push service reads the person's alerts.
threats.mitigation: each message is encrypted for the device (aes128gcm with a fresh key per message); only counts and labels are ever sent

threats.threat: An alert shown on a locked phone reveals private matters to someone nearby.
threats.reason: the digest carries counts and labels only, never amounts or names; the Life OS shows a generic line when discreet mode is on (queue discreet-mode)

threats.threat: Endless subscriptions fill the store or slow each send.
threats.mitigation: at most 10 devices a person (the oldest dropped), 4 KB per subscription, the usual rate limit per device; a device the push service no longer knows is removed on the next send

threats.threat: The new endpoints become a way to read or write the person's state.
threats.mitigation: they touch only the push table; the key file is never served (only the 65-byte public key)
